  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel – Buyer-side review of Seller Update and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**To:** Wattlebridge deal team
**Re:** Where the Seller's package departs from the Buyer's interests, and recommended pushback
**Date:** 6 November 2026

## Headline view

The Seller's covering note describes the package as "fair and balanced". It is not. Read together, the Seller Update and the Disclosure Letter do three things that cut against us:

1. **Compress everything into one weak liability regime** – a 20% cap, 18-month claims window, deductible basket, and "all limitations apply to all Claims" language, with fundamental/title and tax warranties *and* the specific indemnities swept in.
2. **Neutralise the warranties through disclosure and knowledge** – general disclosure of the whole data room *and* public registers, plus a constructive-knowledge bar in cl 8.3. Combined, these would make most warranty claims unwinnable regardless of the cap.
3. **Push known, quantifiable problems past Completion and onto the Buyer** – the AUD 3.2m Riverlark debt (release "following Completion"), the Bluefen consent (30% of revenue, no consent in the data room), the AUD 420k bonuses (not in the funds flow), the Ironquay IP (AUD 180k unpaid, title has not transferred) and the DD-006 privacy incident ("not expected to be material", while the Seller's own letter says they do not know).

Notably, the Disclosure Letter is more candid than the Seller Update. Several points the Update describes as "addressed", "adequate" or "ordinary course" are, in the Seller's own Disclosure Letter, expressly *not* resolved. We should use the Seller's own words against the Seller's positions.

One structural point before the detail: the Disclosure Letter is dated by reference to a **22 September 2026** data room cut-off. We are now six weeks on. Every open item below needs a current status, and the SPA must not permit the Seller to make fresh disclosures against the Completion warranties.

---

## Part A – Liability regime (cll 9.3, 12, 13, 20.5)

### A1. General cap – 20% / AUD 4.8m

**Seller position:** aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims capped at 20%.

**Assessment:** 20% is within market range for general warranties on an unlisted mid-market deal, though at the low end for a target with this many open diligence items. The real problem is not the percentage; it is what the Seller wants to put *under* it (see A4–A6). If the carve-outs are secured, 20–30% is acceptable; if the Seller resists carve-outs, the cap should rise materially.

**Pushback:** Accept 20–30% for general warranties *only*, conditional on the carve-outs below. Flag that we will revisit the figure if W&I insurance is not being used (a W&I policy would not cover the known issues anyway – see Part D).

### A2. De minimis AUD 25k / basket AUD 250k (deductible)

**Seller position:** claims under AUD 25k ignored; nothing recoverable until aggregate exceeds AUD 250k, then only the **excess**.

**Assessment:** The de minimis is high for a AUD 24m deal (≈0.1% of price; 0.05% is more typical). The basket at ≈1.04% is at the top of the range. Most importantly, it is drafted as a **deductible** ("only the excess above the basket is recoverable"), which gives away the first AUD 250k of every loss profile.

**Pushback:**
- De minimis AUD 10,000–12,500, with **related claims or claims arising from the same facts aggregated** for both thresholds.
- Basket AUD 240,000 (1%) or lower, drafted as a **tipping basket** (once exceeded, recover from the first dollar).
- No de minimis or basket for fundamental/title, tax, or specific indemnity claims.

### A3. Time limits – 18 months for all Claims

**Seller position:** general Warranty Claims to be notified within 18 months; **"any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise."**

**Assessment:** 18 months is short; it does not allow a full audit cycle plus investigation. The "applies to all Claims" sentence is the more dangerous element – it is a catch-all designed to pull the title, tax and indemnity claims into the 18-month window and the AUD 4.8m cap.

**Pushback:**
- General warranties: **24 months** (minimum allows two sets of audited accounts).
- Tax warranties and tax indemnity: **7 years** post-Completion (the ATO's standard 4-year amendment period runs from assessment, not Completion, and longer periods apply for fraud/evasion and some entities; 7 years is the conventional Australian position).
- Fundamental/title and capacity warranties: **7 years**, or at minimum the 6-year contractual limitation period under the *Limitation Act 1969* (NSW) running from Completion.
- Specific indemnities: survive until the underlying matter is finally resolved and all periods for third-party claims have expired.
- Time bar should require only **notice** within the period, with a reasonable period (e.g. 9–12 months) thereafter to commence proceedings; any shorter proceedings deadline should be deleted.
- **Delete** the "applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" language and replace with the reverse default: limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims unless expressly extended.

### A4. Fundamental / title / capacity warranties subject to general caps "for administrative simplicity"

**Seller position:** same cap and time limits as general warranties.

**Assessment:** This is the single most aggressive position in the package. "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason. If we do not get the shares we paid for, or the Seller lacked authority to sell them, our loss is the whole price (and more). A AUD 4.8m cap on a AUD 24m title failure is indefensible, and an 18-month window on title is unusual to the point of being a red flag.

**Pushback:** Non-negotiable. Fundamental warranties (title, capacity, authority, no encumbrances over the shares, solvency of the Seller, the Company's share capital) must be:
- Capped at **100% of the purchase price** (plus costs of enforcement);
- Not subject to de minimis, basket, disclosure (general or specific), or the Buyer-knowledge bar;
- Time-limited at 7 years (or 6 years from Completion as an absolute floor).

### A5. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature" (cll 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)

**Seller position:** every limitation, the exclusive-remedy clause and the non-reliance clause apply to all Claims of any nature.

**Assessment:**
- As drafted this would purport to cap and time-bar the Seller's **Completion obligations**, the **specific indemnities**, **leakage/price adjustment** claims, **restraint** breaches, and claims for **fraud or wilful misconduct**. Capping fraud is unenforceable and is routinely rejected; the rest is simply off-market.
- The non-reliance clause cannot exclude statutory liability for misleading or deceptive conduct (s 18 Australian Consumer Law, s 236 damages), but courts will treat such clauses as relevant to reliance and causation. A sweeping version, combined with the knowledge bar and general disclosure, substantially weakens our fall-back position.
- An "exclusive remedy" clause should not deprive us of equitable relief (specific performance/injunctions), termination rights before Completion, or recovery under the Riverlark/Ironquay documents.

**Pushback:** Carve out expressly from all limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance: (i) fraud, dishonesty, wilful concealment or wilful misconduct of the Seller or the Company's management; (ii) fundamental warranties; (iii) tax warranties and tax indemnity; (iv) each specific indemnity; (v) leakage / completion accounts adjustments; (vi) Seller covenants (Completion deliverables, pre-Completion conduct, restraints, confidentiality); (vii) equitable remedies; (viii) non-excludable statutory rights.

### A6. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"

**Seller position:** tax and IP warranties fall under the 20% / 18-month regime.

**Assessment:** Rejected for tax (see A3/A4). Tax exposures surface late and are enforced by a revenue authority, not by the Buyer's choice of timing. An analytics business is also a likely R&D Tax Incentive claimant, which carries clawback and documentation risk. On IP, this business *is* its IP – and the Seller's own Disclosure Letter confirms that title to the SOW3 Project Materials has **not** transferred (see C3).

**Pushback:**
- A full **tax indemnity** for all pre-Completion tax (and tax arising from Completion itself, including on the bonuses), uncapped or capped at 100%, 7 years, not subject to disclosure except the Accounts.
- IP warranties at the higher tier: cap at least 50% of price, 3–4 years, and a **specific indemnity** for the Ironquay matter outside all limitations.

---

## Part B – Disclosure and knowledge (Schedule 7, cl 8.3)

### B1. General disclosure of the data room and public registers

**Seller position:** [1.1] everything in the data room as at 22 Sept 2026 (DD-002 to DD-012) is disclosed; [1.2] also the Accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records".

**Assessment:**
- A blanket data-room disclosure is common in Australia but should be qualified by a **fair disclosure standard**: disclosed only to the extent the fact, matter or circumstance is "fairly disclosed with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter and its likely effect." Without that, a buried line in a spreadsheet "discloses" against every warranty.
- Disclosure of **public registers** (ASIC, PPSR, IP Australia, court lists, land titles) is a classic overreach: it shifts the Seller's duty to disclose onto the Buyer's search budget. Strike it entirely, or limit to specifically listed searches at specified dates annexed to the Letter.
- **DD-001 is missing** from the disclosed range (DD-002 to DD-012). Ask what DD-001 is and why it is excluded.
- **Paragraph 1.3 is missing** from the Letter. Ask for it.
- The Letter contains the odd statement that "all entities, people, transactions and records are fictional". That cannot stand in an executed disclosure letter; require deletion.
- Paragraph [1.4] ("nothing admits breach… or that any consent… is legally required") is standard but, combined with [11] ("Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement"), the Seller is positioning the Letter as a shield while refusing to characterise anything. We should respond in kind: no matter is disclosed against the fundamental warranties, the tax warranties/indemnity or any specific indemnity, and nothing in the Letter is disclosed against the Completion-date repetition of warranties except by a separate Completion Disclosure Letter that the Buyer has a right to reject (with termination/price-adjustment consequences).

**Pushback:** Fair disclosure standard; delete public-register disclosure; disclosure only operates against general warranties; freeze data room index and require a USB/hash-verified copy annexed; no general disclosure against Completion repetition.

### B2. Buyer knowledge bar – cl 8.3

**Seller position:** no claim for any matter of which the Buyer "or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records."

**Assessment:** This is a **constructive knowledge** exclusion. It would bar claims for matters nobody actually knew about, provided a diligent reader *could* have found them. Layered on top of B1, it means the Seller gets two bites: general disclosure of the data room, and a knowledge bar for anything "discoverable" from it. It also extends to advisers' knowledge, which a buyer cannot control. The Seller's own [1.4] disclaims any obligation to characterise what it has disclosed – yet cl 8.3 would bind us to have understood it.

**Pushback:** Delete cl 8.3. If a knowledge qualifier must survive, confine it to the **actual knowledge** of three to four named Wattlebridge deal-team individuals of a matter **fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter**, with no imputation from advisers and no "discoverable" standard. No knowledge qualifier for fundamental, tax or indemnity claims.

---

## Part C – Known issues the Seller is pushing onto the Buyer

### C1. Bluefen consent (cl 3 / 6.3; Disclosure para 2)

**Seller Update says:** consent "is addressed"; Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the condition as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

**Disclosure Letter says:** Bluefen is ~AUD 3.6m / ~30% of FY26 revenue; the contract has a change-control clause (11.2) with **conditions in 11.3**; the Seller has **not** included a final written consent or evidence that the conditions are satisfied.

**Assessment:** Not "addressed". A 30% customer with a change-of-control right is the single largest value risk in this deal. "Reasonable endeavours" is the lowest effort standard. The satisfaction test ("delivery of written consent") ignores the 11.3 conditions – a consent that is itself conditional on, say, price concessions, a term reset or a termination-for-convenience right would satisfy the Seller's drafting while destroying the value we are paying for.

**Pushback:**
- Condition precedent **for the Buyer's benefit only**, waivable only by the Buyer.
- Satisfied only on delivery of Bluefen's **unconditional written consent in a form approved by the Buyer** (acting reasonably), confirming the agreement continues on existing terms, no termination right arises from the transaction, and all 11.3 conditions are satisfied or waived by Bluefen.
- Seller obligation at **best endeavours / all reasonable endeavours**, with Buyer right to participate in Bluefen discussions.
- Specific warranty that no Bluefen termination, non-renewal, dispute or price renegotiation notice has been received, repeated at Completion.
- If timing forces Completion before consent: a **retention/escrow sized to the revenue at risk** (indicatively AUD 3.0–3.6m) released on consent, with price reduction if Bluefen terminates or re-prices within 12 months.
- Material adverse change condition that captures loss or notice of loss of Bluefen.

### C2. Riverlark Bank facility (cl 2 / 7; Disclosure para 3)

**Seller Update says:** ~AUD 3.2m facility "will be addressed by a release to be provided **following** Completion."

**Disclosure Letter says:** not repaid; no final discharge of security; facility has change-of-control (8.1) and discharge (9.2) provisions.

**Assessment:** Inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free deal and unacceptable on its own terms. Completing with the facility live means (i) the Company is in default under 8.1 the moment we complete, (ii) the bank's security remains over the Company's assets (and we should check whether it extends to the **shares** – a share mortgage from Harbourglass would also impeach title), (iii) we are relying on the Seller's post-Completion covenant to procure a release from a third-party bank, and (iv) the AUD 3.2m is not reflected in the price mechanics.

**Pushback:**
- Riverlark repaid **at Completion out of the purchase price**, directed by the funds flow to the bank's nominated account.
- **Payoff letter** from Riverlark delivered pre-Completion, stating the exact payout figure (including break costs and fees), confirming that on receipt the bank will release all security and that no change-of-control default will be asserted.
- Executed **deed of release** and PPSR financing change statements (or an irrevocable undertaking to lodge within a fixed number of business days) as **Completion deliverables**.
- Confirm no other encumbrances (PPSR search on the Company and on Harbourglass for interests over the shares) and a warranty that the Company has no financial indebtedness at Completion other than items in the agreed Debt schedule.
- Debt definition to include break costs, accrued interest, guarantees given for Seller group obligations, and any bank guarantee facilities (e.g. for the office lease).

### C3. Ironquay Development Studio IP (cl 11.1; Disclosure para 4)

**Seller Update says:** existing indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment and "considered adequate".

**Disclosure Letter says:** DD-004 cl 7.3 transfers SOW3 Project Materials only on cleared payment of **every** SOW3 fee; AUD 180k is recorded as open; no receipt and no confirmatory assignment is in the data room; the ledger is not independent verification.

**Assessment:** The indemnity is scoped to the wrong loss. AUD 180k is the cost of the payment; the real exposure is that the Company **does not own** the SOW3 deliverables. If those materials are embedded in the product, Ironquay could assert ownership, license to a competitor, or seek an injunction – losses that dwarf AUD 180k and that an indemnity "limited to the SOW3 payment" would not cover. We also do not know whether other SOWs (1, 2) have the same vesting mechanism and whether they were fully paid.

**Pushback:**
- **Completion deliverable (or CP):** Ironquay's written acknowledgement that all SOW3 fees are paid, together with an **executed confirmatory deed of assignment** of all Project Materials under every SOW, including moral rights consents from Ironquay personnel and a release of any lien.
- The AUD 180k (if genuinely outstanding) is a Seller cost: either paid by the Company pre-Completion and treated as Debt/deducted, or paid out of the price via the funds flow.
- Replace the existing indemnity with a **specific indemnity** for all loss arising from the Company not having full, unencumbered title to any Ironquay deliverable (including third-party claims, re-engineering costs and lost profits), **outside** the general cap, basket, time limits, disclosure and knowledge bar.
- Full IP chain-of-title warranties: all contractors and employees have assigned IP; no open-source copyleft contamination; registered IP schedule.

### C4. Completion bonuses – AUD 420k (DD-005; funds flow)

**Seller Update says:** "a matter for the Seller and not separately itemised in the funds flow."

**Disclosure Letter says:** conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420k, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions; not in the funds flow; silent on payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs.

**Assessment:** If the bonuses are payable by **Paperbark** (as DD-005 implies), then after Completion they are a liability of a company we own. "A matter for the Seller" is only true if the Seller pays them, and the funds flow does not show that. On-costs are material: superannuation guarantee is now 12% (from 1 July 2025), NSW payroll tax is 5.45%, plus PAYG withholding and possibly leave loading – realistically the gross cost is AUD 480–500k. The "continued-employment" condition is also a risk-shift: if payment is deferred and conditional on post-Completion service, the cost crystallises on our watch, and if we dismiss a participant we may trigger a payout or a claim.

**Pushback:**
- Treat all transaction bonuses, retention payments and associated employer on-costs as **Transaction Costs / Debt-like items** deducted from the price (or paid by the Seller directly, with a gross-up indemnity).
- Itemise them in the funds flow with the on-cost calculation.
- Specific indemnity for any claim by a participant and for any employer tax on the payments.
- Confirm there are no other transaction-triggered entitlements (change-of-control terms in executive contracts, option acceleration, ESOP cash-outs) and schedule them.

### C5. DD-006 export / privacy incident (cl 4.6 / Sch 6)

**Seller Update says:** "preliminary operational matter… not expected to be material."

**Disclosure Letter says:** a download link was sent to an unintended external address; ~1,240 records of names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps; unknown whether accessed; investigation preliminary; **not characterised as a confirmed breach**; no loss estimate.

**Assessment:** The Seller is asking us to accept "not material" while telling us in writing that it does not know the scope, access or notification position. Names and business email addresses are personal information under the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth). Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme the Company must complete a reasonable and expeditious assessment within **30 days** of suspecting an eligible data breach; 22 September was 45 days ago, so that assessment should by now be concluded and documented. If the data belongs to a **customer** (quite possibly Bluefen, as an analytics provider), there is also contractual exposure – notification obligations, audit rights, indemnities and termination rights under the customer contract – and reputational risk to the very relationship in C1. Civil penalty exposure under the Privacy Act is now substantial following the 2022 and 2024 reforms (including the new statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy in force since June 2025).

**Pushback:**
- Immediate information request: the completed NDB assessment, incident log, confirmation whether the recipient deleted/confirmed non-access, whose data it is, and whether any customer or regulator has been notified.
- Pre-Completion covenant to complete the assessment, notify OAIC/individuals/customers where required, and consult the Buyer before deciding not to notify.
- **Specific indemnity** for all loss arising from the DD-006 incident (regulatory penalties, notification costs, customer claims, remediation, legal costs), outside all limitations.
- Data protection and cyber warranties (compliance with APPs, no other incidents, security practices), unqualified by the DD-006 disclosure except as to the specific facts disclosed.
- Consider a small retention until the assessment and any notification process is closed.

### C6. Sandbar supplier renewals – 3 × AUD 110k (DD-008 / DD-011)

**Seller Update says:** ordinary-course operating costs.

**Disclosure Letter says:** three "related" renewals of AUD 110k each; "read together for timing/scope"; the Seller does not state whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.

**Assessment:** Three identical AUD 110k commitments, described as related and to be read together, look like a single AUD 330k commitment split into pieces – potentially to sit under a conduct-of-business consent threshold. Whether they are "ordinary course" depends on whether the Company would have renewed anyway, whether the services are needed post-Completion, and whether the cash goes out before or after Completion.

**Pushback:**
- Request the contracts, renewal dates, termination rights and whether any amounts are prepaid or accrued.
- Pre-Completion covenants: Buyer consent required for any commitment above a threshold (e.g. AUD 50k), **aggregating related commitments**.
- If the renewals fall due pre-Completion and are not demonstrably necessary, they are Seller's cost; if prepaid, treat as working capital in completion accounts; if accrued and unpaid, Debt-like.

### C7. Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)

Lower priority, but do not take the Seller's characterisation on trust:
- **Lease:** obtain the lease and confirm whether the "notification obligation" is in fact a change-of-control consent (many commercial leases treat a change in control of a corporate tenant as an assignment). Require notice to be given pre-Completion and a warranty that no landlord consent is required or, if it is, obtain it. Confirm whether any bank guarantee supporting the lease is under the Riverlark facility (links to C2).
- **Mossvale:** an assignment restriction normally does not bite on a share sale, but we must read DD-009 ourselves for any change-of-control definition. Warranty that no counterparty consent is required for the transaction other than those scheduled.

### C8. Title to shares (DD-012)

**Seller Update says:** title is "evidenced by" the share register.

**Disclosure Letter says:** the register identifies the source relied on; the Buyer has not completed its own verification.

**Assessment:** A share register is prima facie – not conclusive – evidence of title (*Corporations Act* s 176). The Seller is quietly shifting verification risk to us while simultaneously trying to cap title warranties at 20% / 18 months (A4). We should do our own ASIC and PPSR searches, confirm no options, convertible notes, SAFE instruments, employee equity or shareholder agreements exist, and confirm Harbourglass's own authority (fund documents, investment committee approvals) and solvency.

**Pushback:** Uncapped title warranties (A4), warranty of no options/convertibles/encumbrances, delivery at Completion of share certificates (or lost-certificate indemnity), executed transfer, board minutes approving registration, and resignations/ASIC forms.

---

## Part D – Structural protections

The known items alone are significant relative to price: AUD 3.2m debt, ~AUD 0.5m bonuses with on-costs, AUD 0.18m Ironquay, AUD 0.33m Sandbar, plus unquantified Bluefen and DD-006 exposure. Given that, and that the Seller is a venture vehicle likely to distribute proceeds to investors shortly after Completion, warranty protection on paper is only as good as the Seller's capacity to pay. Recommend:

1. **Price mechanics:** confirm the debt-free/cash-free mechanism is backed by completion accounts (or a locked box with a robust leakage indemnity and a verified balance sheet). Debt definition must capture Riverlark, bonuses and on-costs, Ironquay arrears, accrued but unpaid Sandbar amounts, and unpaid pre-Completion tax.
2. **Retention / escrow:** 10–15% of price (indicatively AUD 2.4–3.6m) held for 18–24 months to back general claims, with **separate** earmarked retentions for Bluefen (if consent is not obtained pre-Completion) and DD-006 until closed out.
3. **Seller covenant strength:** parent/fund guarantee or restriction on Harbourglass distributing below a stated net asset threshold for the claims period.
4. **W&I insurance:** worth pricing, but note that insurers will exclude every known matter (Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, bonuses, DD-006, Sandbar). W&I can replace the Seller's *general* cap; it does not replace the specific indemnities and Completion deliverables above.
5. **Bring-down:** warranties repeated at Completion; no Seller right to update disclosure against Completion warranties without giving the Buyer a termination or price-adjustment right; MAC condition.
6. **Restraints and key people:** non-compete/non-solicit from Harbourglass and relevant principals; identify key employees (particularly the DD-005 bonus recipients) and confirm retention arrangements.

---

## Summary of recommendations (prioritised)

**Must-have (walk-away items):**
1. Fundamental/title/capacity warranties: 100% cap, no basket/de minimis, 7 years, not subject to disclosure or knowledge bar. Reject "administrative simplicity".
2. Riverlark repaid at Completion from the price, with payoff letter pre-Completion and release/PPSR discharge as Completion deliverables. No post-Completion release.
3. Bluefen: Buyer-only CP satisfied by unconditional consent in Buyer-approved form with cl 11.3 conditions satisfied; retention/price adjustment if we complete without it.
4. Ironquay: paid-up confirmation and confirmatory IP assignment as a Completion deliverable; specific indemnity for title failure outside all limitations.
5. Delete the "all limitations apply to all Claims" default and the "all Claims of any nature" extension of cll 9.3/12.8/20.5; carve out fraud, fundamentals, tax, specific indemnities, covenants and equitable relief.
6. Delete cl 8.3 constructive knowledge; delete disclosure of public registers; impose a fair-disclosure standard.

**Strongly recommended:**
7. Tax: full indemnity, 7 years, 100% cap. IP: higher-tier cap and period.
8. Bonuses (AUD 420k + on-costs) itemised in funds flow as Seller cost/Debt-like with gross-up indemnity.
9. DD-006: completed NDB assessment now; pre-Completion covenants; specific indemnity outside limitations; retention until closed.
10. General regime: 24 months; de minimis ~AUD 10–12.5k with aggregation; 1% tipping (not deductible) basket; 20–30% cap conditional on the carve-outs.
11. Retention/escrow of 10–15% plus Seller covenant support; price W&I as a supplement, not a substitute.

**Housekeeping / information requests:**
12. Current status of every open item (letter is six weeks stale); DD-001 and missing para 1.3; remove the "fictional" statement; Sandbar contracts and termination rights; lease change-of-control analysis; Mossvale clause text; ASIC/PPSR searches on the Company and Harbourglass; schedule of all transaction-triggered employee entitlements.

Our overall response to the Seller should make the point directly: their Disclosure Letter confirms that the consent, the debt, the IP, the bonuses and the incident are all unresolved. A package that leaves each of them unresolved *and* subjects them to a 20% / 18-month / deductible regime with constructive-knowledge and public-register disclosure is not a balanced allocation of risk – it is a transfer of all known risk to the Buyer at a price negotiated on a clean, debt-free basis.

*This memorandum is an issues-based review for the deal team to support instructions to external counsel; clause-by-clause drafting should be settled against the full SPA text, which we have not yet seen in this round.*
=== END ADVICE ===
